examples.question_text:
The table shows direct distances, in kilometres, between four towns. A railway network will connect all four towns at a construction cost of $\$60\,000$ per kilometre. Draw a minimum spanning tree and calculate the minimum construction cost.

| From/To | $A$ | $B$ | $C$ | $D$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $A$ | – | 4.2 | 6.4 | 3.1 |
| $B$ | 4.2 | – | 5.3 | 2.2 |
| $C$ | 6.4 | 5.3 | – | 4.6 |
| $D$ | 3.1 | 2.2 | 4.6 | – |

A minimum spanning tree connecting six picnic areas has five path lengths: $20\text{ m}$, $25\text{ m}$, $30\text{ m}$, $35\text{ m}$ and $40\text{ m}$. Paving costs $\$90$ per metre. Calculate the minimum total path length and paving cost.
examples.solution_text:
The minimum spanning tree is supplied, so sum its five edge weights.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Minimum length} &=20+25+30+35+40\\&=150\text{ m}\end{aligned}$
Multiply by the paving rate.
$\begin{aligned}\text{Minimum cost} &=150\times90\\&=\$13\,500\end{aligned}$

coverage.summary: Authored three examples covering all four distinct assessed methods. Question and solution fields are separate; prose remains editable and inherits automatic solution blue. Diagrams use black ink, explicit 10 pt labels and solution-only tree selections. Calculations use aligned relation gutters. Practice and quiz mathematics were neither changed nor re-audited. Independent example review and actual rendered visual verification remain subsequent stages.

examples.derivation: Independently ordering the edges gives AB=5, EF=6, BD=7, DE=8 and AC=9. Each joins separate components; together they connect all six vertices without a cycle. Their total is 5+6+7+8+9=35 km. The solution diagram contains exactly these five edges with matching weights. This adapts the connector example at lines 424–442 and images 58–59 using different values.

The symmetric table defines six undirected edges. Select BD=2.2 and AD=3.1; AB=4.2 would close triangle ABD, so omit it. CD=4.6 then connects C more cheaply than BC=5.3 or AC=6.4. The minimum length is 2.2+3.1+4.6=9.9 km and construction cost is 9.9×60000=$594000. The solution diagram matches this tree. The table-to-tree and cost method follows lines 503–530.

The supplied minimum spanning tree has five edges for six sites. Summing gives 20+25+30+35+40=150 m; multiplying by the uniform paving rate gives 150×90=$13500. No diagram is necessary because the tree lengths are supplied. Summation follows lines 434–442 and the paving application follows lines 493–501.

review.summary: All four assessed methods are correctly distinguished and covered by the three examples. All 24 exact assessment locators have mappings; accepted assessment mathematics was not re-audited. There are no existing examples to inspect and no syllabus exception is needed. Separate editable fields, inline aligned mathematics, relation gutters and solution-only tree selections satisfy the supplied conventions. Final rendered colour and label-size verification remains for the later visual stage.
